data: How AssetHoard plugins work under the hood
AssetHoard 0.3.1 adds plugins, starting with HEIC photos and a Godot editor bridge. Why we built them on a sandboxed V8 engine, what a plugin can and can't touch, and what happens when one breaks.
The Plugins page in AssetHoard settings, showing the Installed and Browse tabs, the Install from file button and the Godot plugin card

There are two kinds so far. File handlers teach AssetHoard a new file format, so files like HEIC photos import with thumbnails, previews and export like any built-in type. Engine bridges connect AssetHoard to another tool, like the Godot plugin, which lets you browse and import from your library inside the Godot editor.
Are AssetHoard plugins safe to install?

Plugins run in a sandbox with no access to your files, network or other programs by default. A plugin only gets extra abilities through narrow permissions that AssetHoard builds and enforces itself, and you see every permission in plain language before you install. Registry downloads are signature and checksum verified.
Will a broken plugin crash AssetHoard or ruin an import?

No. Each plugin runs separately with its own time and memory limits. If one hangs or crashes, your file still imports, just without a thumbnail, and Reimport fills it in once the plugin is fixed. Other plugins and built-in formats keep working.
Can I write my own AssetHoard plugin?

Yes. Plugins are JavaScript modules, optionally with WebAssembly inside, and one package runs on Windows, macOS and Linux. An SDK with TypeScript types, a scaffold and a test tool is on the way. Until then the HEIC and Godot plugins are good starting points.

Every week someone asks whether AssetHoard can read format X, or talk to engine Y. Plenty of those we can't build into the app. The decoder is a huge C library under a licence we don't want to link, or the engine integration has to be written in another language. And if we built in every one we could, the app would bloat fast.

AssetHoard 0.3.1 adds plugins to handle those requests. The hard part was letting other people's code run inside the app without giving it access to your machine, so most of this post is about that.

The first two plugins

We started with two plugins that work in completely different ways.

HEIC: a new file format

HEIC is the format iPhones save photos in, and a lot of reference images arrive that way. The decoder, libheif, is a big C library. The plugin is libheif compiled to WebAssembly, wrapped in a small amount of JavaScript.

The plugin tells AssetHoard which extensions it handles and what kind of asset they become. Then it registers a hook that takes a file and returns raw pixels.

export async function activate(ctx) {
  ctx.registerFileHandler({
    decode(file) { /* -> { width, height, pixels } */ },
    describe(file) { /* cheap, header only -> metadata */ },
  });
}

AssetHoard handles everything after that in Rust. The plugin knows nothing about thumbnails, the large preview or Export As PNG. HEIC files work everywhere built-in formats do: folder import, watched folders, archives, bundle covers, reimport and export.

The plugin never sees a file path either. It gets a handle it can read from during one call, and it can't open anything else on your disk.

Godot: an editor bridge with no plugin code

The Godot plugin has no JavaScript in it. It's a manifest, a Godot editor addon and one permission.

Install it, pick your Godot project, and an "AssetHoard" tab appears in the editor next to 2D, 3D and Script. You can browse bundles, search with the same filters as the app, and import into whichever folder you have selected in Godot.

The permission tells AssetHoard to start a small local API, which AssetHoard runs itself. The plugin doesn't open any connections. AssetHoard also copies the addon into your project, after checking the folder is a Godot project. The plugin itself has no write access to anything.

Why an embedded V8, not Python or a subprocess

These are the options we ruled out:

Option Why not
Embedded Python No real in-process sandbox, and native packages need builds for every platform
Python on WebAssembly Loses native packages, so codecs like HEIC become impractical
Lua or QuickJS No WebAssembly, so codecs can't be plugins
JavaScript embedded in the app via a webview Every byte would pass between the UI and Rust, and we keep heavy data in Rust
A separate program per plugin Builds for every platform, code-signing problems, and no sandbox by default

We embedded V8, Chrome's JavaScript engine, through deno_core. That's the engine layer Deno is built on, without the rest of Deno. On its own it runs standard JavaScript and WebAssembly, and has no other abilities until we add them.

That gave us three things we needed:

  • No access by default. A new engine instance can't touch files, the network or other processes.
  • WebAssembly support. A C codec ships as a .wasm file inside the plugin.
  • One package for every platform. The same plugin runs on Windows, macOS and Linux, so authors don't need separate builds.

It adds a few megabytes to the installer, and a plugin starts in under 20 milliseconds. An installed plugin doesn't load until you import one of its files.

Permissions are doors we build

A plugin with no permissions can only read the file AssetHoard gives it, its own bundled files and its settings. HEIC needs nothing more, so it asks for no permissions.

Anything beyond that needs a permission. Each permission is a narrow, specific ability that AssetHoard implements and enforces. Take Godot. A general "write files" permission would have been simpler for us to build, but you'd be trusting the plugin with your whole disk. Instead you pick the folder, AssetHoard checks it, and AssetHoard copies only the files the plugin declared.

Only a couple of permissions exist today, and more are designed. Each one ships with tests that check a plugin without the permission gets an error.

A plugin can misbehave, the app shouldn't notice

We plan for two kinds of bad plugin: a buggy one that hangs, leaks memory or crashes, and a hostile one that tries to break out of the sandbox.

For the buggy kind, every plugin runs separately, with a time limit on each call and a memory cap. Runaway loops get stopped. A plugin that fails repeatedly is paused for a while. Plugins also run alongside the normal import pipeline, so a stuck plugin doesn't hold up built-in formats or other plugins.

A plugin failure also never fails your import. The file still comes in without a thumbnail, and right-click > Reimport adds it once the plugin is fixed.

For the hostile kind, the sandbox is the first line of defence, and we update V8 promptly when security fixes land. Registry downloads are signed and checksum verified. Submissions that ask for more permissions get a closer review. If a plugin turns out to be harmful, we can withdraw it and AssetHoard switches it off immediately.

Fewer prompts

If an app asks for permission too often, people stop reading and click yes. So AssetHoard asks once, in plain language, when you install.

  • One prompt, at install. It lists what the plugin can do, which file types it reads, and anything it installs into another tool. There are no per-file or per-session prompts.
  • Updates only flag what changed. If an update doesn't ask for anything new, you just confirm it.
  • No restarts. Install, update, enable and disable all take effect immediately.
  • Settings without code. A plugin lists its settings and AssetHoard builds the form.
  • Warnings that match the risk. A plugin installed from a file gets a small tag. Plenty of game developers install plugins by hand or write their own, so we don't treat it as an emergency.

What's next

We built the plugin API so new kinds of plugin can be added the same way, each with its permissions designed before it ships.

On the list: more file formats, plugins that add actions to the right-click menu, and the one people ask about most, plugins that run after import, such as tagging new textures with an AI model running on your own machine. That one needs things the sandbox doesn't allow yet, so it'll take more work. We'll write about it when it's ready.

We're not giving dates for any of these. Whatever we add, plugins will still start with no access, and each new permission will be narrow, tested and explained at install.

Try it

Plugins are in AssetHoard 0.3.1. Open Settings > Plugins, browse the registry, and install HEIC or Godot. The plugins docs have the details. If you want to build your own, an SDK with TypeScript types, a scaffold and a test tool is on the way. Tell us what you'd build first. These two came straight from requests.

How we built the AssetHoard MCP server
AssetHoard's built-in MCP server lets Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code and Windsurf search your asset library and export into your game project. How we built it.
Diagram showing AI assistants (Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code, Windsurf) searching an AssetHoard library through its MCP server and exporting assets into Godot, Unity and Unreal Engine projects
What is the AssetHoard MCP server?

It's a small server built into the AssetHoard desktop app that speaks the Model Context Protocol (MCP), the open standard AI tools use to talk to other programs. When it's switched on, AI clients such as Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code, Windsurf and Claude Desktop can search your asset library, look at thumbnails, browse bundles, tags and projects, and copy assets into your game project. Optional write tools let them organise the library and import files too.
Which AI clients work with AssetHoard's MCP server?

Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code and Windsurf connect directly over HTTP using the setup snippet from Settings > MCP Server. Claude Desktop only launches local stdio servers, so for now it connects through the mcp-remote bridge, which needs Node.js.
Is the AssetHoard MCP server safe to leave running?

It's off by default and built to be boring from a security point of view. It only listens on 127.0.0.1, so nothing on your network can reach it. Every request needs a 48-character random token. Requests from web browsers are refused outright, which blocks DNS rebinding attacks. Write tools are a separate opt-in, imports need you to click Allow in the app, exports never overwrite files, and every change the assistant makes can be undone with Ctrl+Z.
Can an AI assistant delete my assets through MCP?

No. There are no tools for deleting assets or bundles. The only deletes are for categories nothing uses and projects that are already empty. Everything else the write tools do goes on AssetHoard's normal undo stack, labelled with MCP:, so you can reverse it.
Does AssetHoard need to be open for the MCP server to work?

Yes. The server runs inside the app, so close AssetHoard and the tools go away. That's deliberate: it means there's only ever one program writing to your library database, and the open window updates live when the assistant changes something.
Does the MCP server send my files to an AI company?

AssetHoard itself never sends anything off your machine. The assistant sees what the tools return: names, paths, tags, categories, metadata and small preview images. Your AI client then sends that to its model provider like any other context, so treat it the same way you'd treat pasting a file listing into a chat. Raw file contents are only copied into a folder you name, on your own disk.

You're three hours into building a level. You need a barrel. You know you own at least four barrel packs, because you bought them in three different bundle sales and one of them was "a steal". Finding them means leaving the editor, opening a file browser, and digging through folders called Downloads (2).

Meanwhile there's an AI assistant sitting in your editor that can write a state machine in eight seconds but has no idea what's on your hard drive.

AssetHoard is a local-first desktop asset manager for indie game developers and digital artists, and version 0.2.3 fixes that with a built-in MCP server. This post covers how we built it, why it's locked down the way it is, and the things we've found it genuinely useful for.

What MCP is, briefly

The Model Context Protocol is an open standard for letting AI tools call other programs. A program exposes a set of named tools with typed arguments ("search", "export", "create_bundle"), and any MCP client (Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code, Windsurf, Claude Desktop) can discover and call them.

For an asset manager that's a natural fit. AssetHoard already knows every model, texture, sprite and sound you own, what's in which bundle, what it's tagged, and what each file depends on. MCP lets your assistant ask it.

The decisions that shaped it

Built into the app, not a separate program

The obvious shortcut would have been a little standalone server that opens AssetHoard's SQLite database and reads it directly. We didn't do that, for two reasons.

First, two programs writing to one SQLite file is how you end up with a corrupted library and a very bad afternoon. Second, the app would never find out about changes. You'd ask your assistant to tag forty rocks and the open window would keep showing them untagged until you restarted.

So the server runs inside AssetHoard itself, and the app has to be open for it to answer. That turned out to be a feature: every change the assistant makes shows up in the window straight away.

Living inside the app also means you stay in charge of it from the app:

  • Turn it on and off. One switch in Settings > MCP Server. It's off until you flip it, and a plug icon sits in the toolbar whenever it's running, so you're never guessing.
  • See what changed. When an assistant exports files or edits your library, AssetHoard shows a notification in the app saying what it did, and the settings page keeps a list of recent calls.
  • Decide how much the assistant can do. Out of the box it can only search, look and export. Changing your library needs "Allow write tools" switched on, and importing files pops up a prompt you have to approve. If you'd rather keep it read-only forever, just leave the write switch off.

One rule: MCP never touches the database directly

The MCP code lives in its own module, and it isn't allowed to call app commands or SQL. Everything goes through a small internal library API that sits underneath both the UI and the MCP server.

That sounds like bureaucracy, but it's what makes the write tools trustworthy. When an assistant moves an asset into a bundle, it runs exactly the same function as when you drag it there yourself. Same validation, same audit log, same undo entry. There's no second, slightly different code path quietly drifting out of sync with the real one.

It also makes adding a tool cheap. A new tool is a typed argument struct (whose doc comments become the descriptions the model reads) and a thin method that calls the library API. The interesting logic stays in one place and gets tested once.

Rust, rmcp and streamable HTTP

AssetHoard's backend is Rust, so we used rmcp, the official Rust SDK for MCP, with its streamable HTTP transport mounted on axum. Database work runs on blocking worker threads so a big search never stalls the app's async runtime, and each call is recorded in a recent-activity list you can watch in Settings.

We picked HTTP over stdio because the server lives inside a desktop app that's already running. Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code and Windsurf all connect to a local HTTP endpoint with a header, which is a one-line setup. Claude Desktop is the odd one out: it only launches stdio servers, so for now it connects through the mcp-remote bridge.

A fixed port, on purpose

The server listens on port 47823 by default. You can change it, but AssetHoard will never pick a different one on its own if that port is busy. Auto-switching sounds helpful until every client config you've written silently stops matching. Instead, a taken port shows up as an error with a readable message, and you choose what to do.

Making it safe to leave on

A local server that can read your files and write to your library deserves some paranoia. Here's what's in place:

  • Off by default. You turn it on in Settings > MCP Server.
  • Local only. It binds to 127.0.0.1, so nothing on your network or the internet can reach it.
  • Token required. Every request needs a bearer token: 48 random hex characters, compared in constant time. Regenerating it disconnects every client.
  • Browsers are refused. Any request with an Origin header is rejected, and the Host header must be a loopback address. Browsers always send Origin; CLI and IDE clients don't. This blocks DNS rebinding, where a malicious web page tries to talk to a server on your machine, and it's what the MCP spec asks local servers to do.
  • Write tools are a second opt-in. "Allow write tools" is a separate toggle, and it's checked on every call, so switching it off takes effect immediately, even for clients that are already connected.
  • No deleting your stuff. There are no tools for deleting assets or bundles. The only deletes are for categories nothing uses and projects that are already empty.
  • Exports never overwrite. If a file already exists at the destination, it's skipped and reported.
  • Imports ask first. When an assistant wants to import a folder, AssetHoard pops up a prompt with the path, file count, size and target bundle, and flashes the window. No answer within 60 seconds counts as no. If you trust your setup, "Import without asking" turns this off.
  • Everything is undoable. Writes go on the normal undo stack with an MCP: label, like MCP: Moved 1 asset into 'Rocks', and a toast tells you what changed. Ctrl+Z (Cmd+Z on a Mac) works exactly as it does for your own edits.

A plug icon appears in the toolbar whenever the server is running, so you always know it's on.

Small things that made a big difference

Search returns text, thumbnails are separate. Search results are ids, names, types, paths and tags, which keeps them small. If the assistant wants to actually look at something, it calls get_thumbnail and gets a preview image of at most 256 pixels. That means it can check that the "mossy rock" really is mossy before suggesting it, without flooding its context with every result's picture.

Dependencies come along. Exporting a model brings its textures. Exporting a Godot .tres brings the files it references, and Unreal assets bring theirs. Exporting a whole bundle keeps its folder layout. Assets inside zip archives or .unitypackage files are pulled out first.

Clickable links. Every asset, bundle and project the server returns includes an assethoard:// link. The assistant can hand you a link, you click it, and AssetHoard jumps to that item. We added the link scheme to the app specifically for this.

Errors the model can read. An unknown id, a bundle inside a package, or write tools being switched off all come back as plain error messages rather than protocol failures, so the assistant can explain what happened or try something else.

What you can do with it

Here's what this looks like in practice. These are the kinds of things you'd type into Claude Code, Cursor or similar with AssetHoard running.

Set dressing without leaving the editor

"Find three different barrel models and a wood texture that matches, and copy them into Assets/Props."

The assistant searches your library, looks at the thumbnails of the best few, picks a set and exports them, textures included. You keep building the level. This was the main use case we designed for, and it's the one in the demo video.

Search by what it looks like, not what it's called

"Do I have any mossy stone wall textures?"

Search works the same way as AssetHoard's search bar: by name with typo tolerance, and by meaning when semantic search is turned on. Since 0.2.3 that includes embedded audio metadata too, so "glass shatter" can find SFX_0472_FINAL.wav if that's what its description says.

Narrow it down like you would in the app

"Show me Godot UI sprites from my Platformer Kit bundle."

Results can be filtered by file type, asset class, engine, tag, category or bundle. The assistant works out the bundle id itself and filters inside it.

Drop a whole tileset into a project

"Copy my 'Dungeon Tileset' bundle into the Godot project at C:/dev/crawler."

The bundle's sub-bundles become folders in the destination, so the structure you set up in AssetHoard carries over.

Tidy up the library (write tools on)

"Make a bundle called 'Rocks' under 'Environment', move every rock model into it and tag them 'nature'."

The assistant creates the bundle, searches, moves and tags. Each step appears live in the app and is its own undo entry. If it gets carried away and moves a boulder that was actually a potato, Ctrl+Z.

A slower but satisfying variation: "Find the untagged textures in my Downloads bundle, look at each one and suggest tags." Review the suggestions, say yes, and let it apply them.

Keep track of what a game uses

"Start a project called 'Crawler' and add the dungeon tileset and the footstep sounds to it."

Projects in AssetHoard only record references. Nothing moves, and an item can belong to several projects. Once a project is set up, you can ask questions like "list everything in Crawler and tell me which assets have no licence recorded", which is a much nicer way to find out before release than after.

Onboard a new pack

"Import C:/Users/me/Downloads/platformer-kit-v2 into my Platformer Kit bundle, then categorise the new assets by type."

AssetHoard asks you to allow the import, runs it through the normal import queue with the usual progress notification, then the assistant categorises what came in. The whole import is one undo entry.

What's next

The main gap right now is Claude Desktop needing the mcp-remote bridge. A small native shim that lets it connect directly is on the list. We'd also like to hear what you end up using the server for, because the tool list was shaped by our own workflow and yours is probably weirder.

Try it

The MCP server is in AssetHoard 0.2.3 and later. Open Settings > MCP Server, switch it on, and paste the setup command into your client. The MCP docs cover each client, and the tool reference lists every tool and its arguments. AssetHoard is free to download during the open beta, so the only thing it'll cost you is finally finding out how many barrel packs you own.

What is a .yymps file? GameMaker local packages
A .yymps file is a GameMaker local package: a zip of sprites, objects, sounds and more, exported from one project to import into another. How to open one.
AssetHoard library showing GameMaker .yymps packages as bundles, each with a sprite thumbnail, and the details panel open on an animated insect robot sprite

A .yymps file is a GameMaker local package. It is a zip archive holding a selection of resources, such as sprites, objects, scripts, sounds and tilesets, exported from one GameMaker project so they can be imported into another. Many GameMaker Marketplace assets and itch.io packs are distributed as .yymps files.
How do I import a .yymps file into GameMaker?

Open your project, then choose Tools, Import Local Package and select the .yymps file. GameMaker lists every resource in the package so you can tick the ones you want before importing them into the project.
How do I open a .yymps file without GameMaker?

A .yymps is a standard zip archive, so you can open it with 7-Zip, or rename a copy to .zip and open it with your operating system. Inside you will find GameMaker's usual resource folders, with .yy files describing each resource and the PNG frames and audio they use. An asset manager like AssetHoard can also read the package in place and preview the sprites, sounds, tilesets and fonts inside.
What is the difference between .yymps and .yyz?

A .yymps is a local package containing only the resources you chose to export, meant for importing into an existing project. A .yyz is a compressed export of an entire project, meant to be opened as a project in its own right. Both are zip archives.
Why will my .yymps file not import?

The most common cause is a version mismatch. Packages made in a newer version of GameMaker may use resource formats an older version cannot read, so update GameMaker first. Packages from GameMaker Studio 2 before version 2.3 used the older .yymp extension and an older resource format.

A .yymps file is a GameMaker local package: a zip archive holding a selection of resources, such as sprites, objects, scripts, sounds and tilesets, exported from one GameMaker project so they can be imported into another. If you have bought an asset pack for GameMaker on the Marketplace or itch.io, it probably arrived as a .yymps. This post covers what is inside one, how to import and create them, and how to see what a package contains without opening GameMaker.

What is inside a .yymps file?

A .yymps is an ordinary zip file with a GameMaker-specific extension. Open it and you will find:

  • Resource folders laid out the same way as a GameMaker project: sprites/, objects/, sounds/, scripts/, tilesets/, fonts/ and so on.
  • A .yy file for each resource. This is a JSON file describing the resource: a sprite's frames and playback speed, an object's sprite and parent, a sound's audio file and settings.
  • The raw files those resources use, such as the PNG frames of a sprite or the WAV and OGG files behind a sound.
  • A small metadata file describing the package itself.

The .yy files are what tie everything together. On its own, a sprite's .yy is just a list of frame references, and an object's .yy is mostly a pointer to a sprite. GameMaker reads them and rebuilds the resources when you import the package.

How to import a .yymps file into GameMaker

  1. Open the project you want to add the resources to.
  2. Choose Tools, Import Local Package from the menu.
  3. Select the .yymps file.
  4. GameMaker lists every resource in the package. Tick the ones you want and click Import.

The resources land in your Asset Browser like any others. If the package contains a resource with the same name as one already in your project, GameMaker will ask how to handle the clash, so read that dialog carefully before you click through.

How to create a .yymps file

To share resources between your own projects, or to distribute an asset pack:

  1. Open the project that holds the resources.
  2. Choose Tools, Create Local Package.
  3. Fill in the package details, then add the resources you want to include.
  4. Save the package. GameMaker writes a .yymps file you can import anywhere.

Include anything the resources depend on. If you export an object but not the sprite it uses, the object will import with a missing sprite.

.yymps vs .yyz vs .yy

GameMaker uses several similar extensions, and they are easy to mix up:

Extension What it is When you see it
.yymps A local package: chosen resources from a project, zipped Asset packs, Marketplace downloads, sharing resources between projects
.yyz A compressed export of a whole project Sharing or archiving an entire project
.yyp The project file, listing every resource in the project The root of every project folder
.yy A single resource's definition, in JSON One per sprite, object, sound and so on, inside a project or package
.yymp The older package format from GameMaker Studio 2 before version 2.3 Old asset packs

The short version: import a .yymps into a project, open a .yyz as a project.

How to open a .yymps file without GameMaker

Because a .yymps is a zip, any archive tool can open it. Use 7-Zip, or copy the file, rename the copy to .zip and open it in Windows Explorer or macOS Finder.

That shows you the files, but not much more. You will see folders of .yy JSON and PNG frames with names like spr_player_idle, and you have to open frames one at a time to work out what each sprite looks like. Sounds, tilesets and fonts are no easier. For a pack of a few hundred resources, that is a slow way to find the one you want.

Previewing .yymps packages in AssetHoard

AssetHoard reads .yymps packages and .yyz exports in place, without extracting them, and treats the resources inside like any other asset in your library:

  • Sprites play back as animations at their own playback speed.
  • Sounds play straight from the card.
  • Tilesets open with a grid overlay that respects offset and separation.
  • Fonts show their baked atlas.
  • Objects show the sprite they use.

Each resource is filed under the type it actually is, so a GameMaker sprite turns up alongside the rest of your sprites and the normal filters find it. Everything is searchable and taggable, which matters once you own more than a handful of packs. It works with the .yy format used since GameMaker Studio 2.3.

The full details, including how references between resources are resolved and current limitations, are in the GameMaker files documentation. For the overview, see AssetHoard for GameMaker.

If you are weighing up which engine to use in the first place, our GameMaker vs Godot comparison covers the trade-offs.
